### Horse Race: ARIMA vs. ETS

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(BVAR)
library(knitr)

#Read in Data 
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double())
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))
has_gaps(liquor)

#Plots
liquor |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title= "Liquor Sales in Millions of Dollars",
    x= "Month",
    y= "Sales"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(
    title= "Seasonal Plot of Log Sales",
    x= "Month",
    y= "Log Sales") +
  theme_minimal()
#Liquor sales have a strong seasonal and trend pattern with peaks in 
#December and troughs in January. The seasonal swings grow with the level
#suggesting that a log transformation is appropriate. 

#Univariate Models
liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
#An ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1) model and a ETS(A,A,A) model were chosen. The ARIMA
#model is seasonally differenced once and the ETS model has additive components 
#for its trend, seasonality, and error. 

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()
liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6)
#With a p-value of 0 and the acf graph it can be determined that the residuals
#aren't white noise, ie there is still sturctule left to be captured in the data

#Horse Race
liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")

#There are 216 different forecast origins in the TS-CV.

liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
#The first forecast is for January 2002, and the last is December of 2019. The 
#ARIMA model has the lowest RMSE and MAE values, suggesting that it is the best 
#model for forecasting liquor sales.

#DM Test
liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

t1 <- forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets,    h = 1, power = 2)
t2 <- forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)

kable(
  data.frame(
    Comparison   = c("ARIMA vs ETS", "ARIMA vs SNAIVE"),
    `DM statistic` = c(t1$statistic, t2$statistic),
    `p-value`      = c(t1$p.value,   t2$p.value),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 3
)
#From the results of the DM test, which show that the ARIMA model does not
#have equal forecast accuracy to the ETS and SNAIVE models, it can be concluded
#that the ARIMA model is best for forecasting liquor sales. 
```

### Forecast Combination

```{r}
liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
#The combo model does worse than the base ARIMA but performs better than the
#ETS and snaive models. 

cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
#The correlation between the ARIMA and ETS forecast errors is 0.88, 
#which is a strong positive correlation. This suggests that the two models are 
#capturing similar patterns in the data, and combining them may not provide 
#significant improvements in forecast accuracy.
```

### VAR vs. BVAR

```{r}
qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))

growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))
qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),     # real GDP
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),   # real consumption
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),    # real investment
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),    # payroll employment
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),   # GDP price index
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),     # unemployment rate
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),   # federal funds rate
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>    # 10-year Treasury yield
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()
nrow(y)
head(y)

N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)
actual <- y[121:N, ]
#There are 120 forecasts produced for each variable the first forecast will be
#1990 Q1 and the last is 2019 Q4.

var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)            # columns: y_t, then its lags 1 to p
  M <- ncol(z)                    # number of variables
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))   # constant, latest p lags
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}

rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))
rmse_by_var(fc_var1)
rmse_by_var(fc_var4)
#The smaller VAR forecasts better for all variables except inflation. The smaller
#model forecasts better because it has a much lower estimation error. The larger
#VAR has a large number of variables, increasing the estimation error such that
#it overshoots the potential approximation error of using a smaller model.

bvar_cv <- function(lambda) {
  pr <- bv_priors(hyper = "lambda",
                  mn = bv_mn(lambda = bv_lambda(mode = lambda, sd = 0.4,
                                                min = 0.999 * lambda,
                                                max = 1.001 * lambda),
                             b = 0))
  fc <- NULL
  for (T in origins) {
    fit_T <- bvar(y[1:T, ], lags = 4, priors = pr,
                  n_draw = 2000, n_burn = 1000, verbose = FALSE)
    x <- c(1, t(y[T:(T - 3), ]))         # constant and 4 lags of each variable
    fc <- rbind(fc, x %*% coef(fit_T))   # forecast of y_{T+1}
  }
  fc
}

fc_bvar_03 <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_03.rds")

var_results <-readRDS("results/var_results.rds")

var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)

#The BVAR(4) model with lambda = 0.3 performs better than the VAR(4), this is 
#because the BVAR model shrinks the coefficients towards zero which helps clear
#some of the estimation error that is present in the VAR(4) model. Compared to
#the VAR(1) model, the BVAR model does better at modeling investment, inflation,
#and the 10-year treasury yield, but does worse at the other variables. 

#When lambda is set at 0.05 the model performs worse, indicating that there is
#too much shrinkage and the model is not able to capture the dynamics of the 
#data. The model with the lowest RSME doesn't translate to how fairly it will
#forecast out of sample, since the RSME may just be fitting the training sample
#and including noise or variation that isn't relevant in making future
#forecasts.

#DM Test GDP
e_var4_gdp <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar_gdp <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4_gdp, e_bvar_gdp, h = 1, power = 2)

#DM Test Inflation 
e_var4_infl <- actual[, "infl"] - fc_var4[, 5]
e_bvar_infl <- actual[, "infl"] - fc_bvar_03[, 5]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4_infl, e_bvar_infl, h = 1, power = 2)

#The DM test for GDP concludes that the two models don't have equal forecast 
#accuracy, however for inflation the DM test concludes that the two models do 
#have equal forecast accurary. This suggests that while the BVAR model has a
#lower RMSE it doesn't necessarily translate to better forecast accuracy for 
#all variables, or that it is the best model for future forecasts.
```

### Factor Model

```{r}
md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,                      # level
         "2" = d(x),                   # first difference
         "3" = d(d(x)),                # second difference
         "4" = log(x),                 # log
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),        # growth rate
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),     # change in the growth rate
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]
dim(fm)

tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
#INDPRO and PAYEMS are transformed into growth rates, CPIAUCSL is transformed 
#into the change in the growth rate, and FEDFUNDS is transformed into its
#first difference. The federal funds rate is already a rate so it doesn't need 
#to be logged, whilst INDPRO is in levels so it is logged and differenced to get
#the growth rate.

Z <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()
pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))
 
summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]
#The first three factors capture around 30% of the variation in the data 

F1 <- pc$x[, 1] * sign(cor(pc$x[, 1], fm$INDPRO))
tibble(date = fm$date, F1 = F1) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, F1)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "First Factor from FRED-MD", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 1], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 2], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
#The first factor is most correlated with production and employment, the graph
#fluctuates with the business cycle. The second factor is most correlated with
#various inflation measures, thus it captures the inflation trends. 

ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]         # factors using data through T
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
#Estimating the factors once introduce information leakage in the TS-CV causing
#the factor model to lose forecast accuracy. 

direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)      # growth over the next h months
  g  <- lv$g                                      # growth over the latest month
  
  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL")
#The factors do improve the forecast accuracy of the CPIAUCSL series, with a 
#lower RMSE and MAE. The RSME is reduced by around 10%, the difference in the 
#models is statistically significant since the p-value from a DM test is less
#than 0.05.
```

### Reflection

There is a trade off between model complexity and forecast accuracy which was exemplified by the horse races done in this problem set. More complex models may seem appealing, as they can model data more specifically and with more detail, however the more complex a model the more estimation error is introduced reducing its forecasting power in future forecasts. Shrinkage, equal weights, and factors are all methods of reducing the estimation error of models whilst allowing for flexibility in a models structure, allowing them to compete with/out-perform simple benchmark models which trade off complexity for small estimation errors.
